###### Abstract

Incomplete records can sharpen bounds on joint outcome probabilities even when no pair of outcomes is jointly observed. I derive sharp pointwise Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds combining known population marginals with selectively observed records, without restricting the observation mechanism. I establish an exact reduction of the identification problem to finite-dimensional optimization, yielding computable characterizations of both bounds. Illustrations involving income mobility, potential outcomes, and split questionnaires demonstrate how incomplete records can improve identification relative to the classical bounds.

Keywords: Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds; incomplete observations; partial identification; optimal transport; income persistence.   
JEL classification: C02, C14, C18.

## 1 Introduction

Many questions in empirical economics concern the joint behavior of outcomes that are not fully observed. Examples include income persistence across generations, dependence between potential outcomes, and multidimensional economic deprivation. A central difficulty is sample selectivity: whether an outcome is observed may depend on its value or on other, unobserved outcomes. Consequently, the distribution of observed records need not be representative of the population, complicating identification of the joint outcome distribution ([Heckman 1979](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.03075v1#bib.bib18); [Manski 1989](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.03075v1#bib.bib22)). In [computer science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_science "Computer science") and [optimization theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optimization_(mathematics) "Optimization (mathematics)"), the **max-flow min-cut theorem** states that in a [flow network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flow_network "Flow network"), the maximum amount of flow passing from the [_source_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_graph_theory#Direction "Glossary of graph theory") to the [_sink_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_graph_theory#Direction "Glossary of graph theory") is equal to the total weight of the edges in a [minimum cut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_cut "Minimum cut"), i.e., the smallest total weight of the edges which if removed would disconnect the source from the sink.

For example, imagine a network of pipes carrying water from a reservoir (the source) to a city (the sink). Each pipe has a capacity representing the maximum amount of water that can flow through it per unit of time. The max-flow min-cut theorem tells us that the maximum amount of water that can reach the city is limited by the smallest total capacity of any set of pipes that, if cut, would completely isolate the reservoir from the city. This smallest total capacity is the min-cut. So, if there's a bottleneck in the pipe network, represented by a small min-cut, that bottleneck will determine the overall maximum flow of water to the city.

This is a special case of the [duality theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_problem "Dual problem") for [linear programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_program "Linear program") and can be used to derive [Menger's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menger's_theorem "Menger's theorem") and the [Kőnig–Egerváry theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C5%91nig's_theorem_(graph_theory) "Kőnig's theorem (graph theory)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max-flow_min-cut_theorem#cite_note-1)

keenable.title: Valid Inequalities for Bilevel 0-1 Shortest-Path Problems
keenable.snippet: We characterize valid inequalities for bilevel programs in which the leader makes binary decisions, and the follower solves a shortest-path problem. We exploit a dualize-and-combine reformulation and show that even with ideal formulations for the leader and the follower primal solution sets, fractional solutions may still appear in the continuous relaxation. From that reformulation, we identify that the interaction between the leader variables and the follower dual variables, which we capture through a leader–potential set, is the key structure to be convexified to guarantee that a continuous relaxation recovers the optimal value of the original problem, closing the objective gap. Furthermore, we characterize the valid inequalities for the leader–potential set through network flows, and identify a family of inequalities we name *root cuts* that suffice to recover the optimal value.

Maximum Satisfiability (MaxSAT) is an optimization extension of the Satisfiability (SAT) problem. In Branch-and-Bound (BnB) MaxSAT solving, the quality of the lower bound estimation is critical for effective search space pruning. State-of-the-art BnB solvers typically estimate this bound by identifying disjoint inconsistent subformulas (cores) via Unit Propagation (UP). However, a limitation of this standard approach is that UP fails to detect cores that exhibit complex dependencies with already identified cores. In this paper, we propose a further lookahead algorithm that leverages pre-detected cores to uncover additional disjoint inconsistencies, thereby tightening the lower bound. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly tightens the lower bound, enabling the state of the art BnB solver MaxCDCL to solve more instances.

octen.title: A Tight Max-Flow Min-Cut Duality Theorem for Non-Linear Multicommodity   Flows
octen.snippet:
The Max-Flow Min-Cut theorem is the classical duality result for the Max-Flow
problem, which considers flow of a single commodity. We study a multiple
commodity generalization of Max-Flow in which flows are composed of real-valued
k-vectors through networks with arc capacities formed by regions in \R^k. Given
the absence of a clear notion of ordering in the multicommodity case, we define
the generalized max flow as the feasible region of all flow values.
  We define a collection of concepts and operations on flows and cuts in the
multicommodity setting. We study the mutual capacity of a set of cuts, defined
as the set of flows that can pass through all cuts in the set. We present a
method to calculate the mutual capacity of pairs of cuts, and then generalize
the same to a method of calculation for arbitrary sets of cuts. We show that
the mutual capacity is exactly the set of feasible flows in the network, and
hence is equal to the max flow. Furthermore, we present a simple class of the
multicommodity max flow problem where computations using this tight duality
result could run significantly faster than default brute force computations.
  We also study more tractable special cases of the multicommodity max flow
problem where the objective is to transport a maximum real or integer multiple
of a given vector through the network. We devise an augmenting cycle search
algorithm that reduces the optimization problem to one with m constraints in at
most \R^{(m-n+1)k} space from one that requires mn constraints in \R^{mk} space
for a network with n nodes and m edges. We present efficient algorithms that
compute eps-approximations to both the ratio and the integer ratio maximum flow
problems. cs.DS, math.AT M. Broussard, Bala Krishnamoorthy

parallel-fast.snippet:
* • Introduction of a bin-packing variant where each item has both a size and a threshold.
* • Theoretical study of the structural properties of optimal solutions for this problem.
* • Adaptation of three state-of-the-art integer programming formulation.
* • Theoretical study and comparison of the bounds of the proposed formulation.
* • Numerical comparison of the three methods on a diversified benchmark of instances.

Abstract

We present a new variant of one-dimensional bin packing, called the bin packing with thresholds problem. In this scenario, any item is equipped with a size and a threshold, and packing an item into a bin is possible if and only if the remaining capacity is larger than both these item-specific parameters. Thus, the feasibility of a subset of items typically depends on the packing order. This problem originates from a joint production/maintenance scheduling application in which processing jobs deteriorate the condition of the machine, meaning that the threshold constraint represents requirements on the machine’s condition to process a job. In this article, this novel variant of bin packing is investigated from a theoretical and numerical point of view. First, some important structural properties of an optimal solution are derived. Based on these observations, three integer linear programming (ILP) formulations are presented: a basic assignment model, an exponential-size pattern-based approach, and a pseudo-polynomial arcflow formulation. For these approaches, relations between the associated LP bounds are established mathematically. Finally, all three formulations are compared based on extensive numerical experiments involving differently characterized benchmark sets.

Incomplete records can sharpen bounds on joint outcome probabilities even when no pair of outcomes is jointly observed. ## 1. Why Quants Separate Marginals from Dependence

Every joint distribution of two risk factors answers two different questions at once. The first is how each variable behaves on its own: how fat its tails are, whether it is skewed, what its 99th percentile looks like. The second is how the variables move together: whether large losses in one tend to arrive with large losses in the other, and whether that link is stronger in a crash than on a quiet day. A bivariate normal answers both questions with one set of parameters, and that is exactly its weakness. If equity returns have Student-t tails and credit spreads are lognormal, no textbook joint family fits both marginals and the dependence you actually observe.

A copula is the mathematical object that lets you answer the two questions separately. You fit each marginal distribution with whatever model suits it, and then you choose a function that glues those marginals together. ## Why Four CDF Values Determine a Rectangle

A joint cumulative distribution function records probabilities for regions extending from the lower left of the plane. A rectangle is bounded on all four sides, so its probability is not usually a single CDF value. Instead, four corner values combine to retain the probability inside the rectangle while removing the regions outside it. This is useful whenever a problem supplies a joint CDF, particularly when a discrete variable can put positive probability directly on a boundary.

**Definition:** For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), their **joint cumulative distribution function** is $$ F(x,y)=P(X\le x,\ Y\le y). $$ It gives the probability that both variables are at most their specified thresholds. Define the left-limit notation by \(F(x-,y)=\lim_{t\uparrow x}F(t,y)\), \(F(x,y-)=\lim_{t\uparrow y}F(x,t)\), and \(F(x-,y-)=\lim_{s\uparrow x,\ t\uparrow y}F(s,t)\). These limits include values strictly below the relevant threshold rather than values equal to it.

Start with the half-open rectangle \((a,b]\times(c,d]\). The CDF value \(F(b,d)\) includes all outcomes with \(X\le b\) and \(Y\le d\). Subtracting \(F(a,d)\) removes outcomes with \(X\le a\), while subtracting \(F(b,c)\) removes outcomes with \(Y\le c\). The lower-left region \(X\le a,\ Y\le c\) was subtracted twice, so it must be added back once.

$$ P(a<X\le b,\ c<Y\le d) =F(b,d)-F(a,d)-F(b,c)+F(a,c). $$

The four terms are an inclusion-exclusion calculation. Their signs are always \(+,-,-,+\): add the top-right corner, subtract the two adjacent strips, and add back their overlapping lower-left region. This sign pattern is the same whether the distribution is discrete or continuous. What changes with discreteness is which threshold values or left limits belong in the four terms.

## What the Joint CDF Measures

When two random variables describe the same outcome, a probability question can place a threshold on each variable at once. For example, a service center might ask for the probability that processing takes at most two days **and** that the case is not escalated. The joint cumulative distribution function answers this kind of question for any pair of thresholds.

**Definition:** For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), their **joint cumulative distribution function** is

$$ F_{X,Y}(x,y)=P(X\le x,\;Y\le y). $$

The value \(F_{X,Y}(x,y)\) is the probability that both variables are no greater than their respective thresholds.

The event in this definition consists of outcomes whose coordinates satisfy \(X\le x\) and \(Y\le y\). On a graph with \(X\) on the horizontal axis and \(Y\) on the vertical axis, those outcomes lie in the rectangle extending left from \(x\) and down from \(y\). This is called a **lower-left rectangle**. The boundaries at \(x\) and \(y\) are included because the definition uses “less than or equal to.”

The joint CDF is a function of two real thresholds. Its value is a probability, so it must lie between zero and one. Increasing either threshold cannot decrease the value: a larger threshold includes every outcome counted at the smaller threshold, and possibly more. These basic checks are useful when evaluating a proposed formula or calculation.

## Calculating from a Discrete Joint Distribution

For discrete random variables, the joint distribution assigns probability to possible pairs of values. To find \(F_{X,Y}(x,y)\), include every pair \((a,b)\) for which \(a\le x\) and \(b\le y\), then add the probabilities of those pairs. The thresholds need not themselves be possible values of either random variable.

When an insurer tracks two losses together, a probability statement may concern both at once: for example, the chance that one loss is within a specified range while another also falls within its own range. Incomplete records can sharpen bounds on joint outcome probabilities even when no pair of outcomes is jointly observed. I derive sharp pointwise Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds combining known population marginals with selectively observed records, without restricting the observation mechanism. ultimate.snippet: We characterize valid inequalities for bilevel programs in which the leader makes binary decisions, and the follower solves a shortest-path problem. We exploit a dualize-and-combine reformulation and show that even with ideal formulations for the leader and the follower primal solution sets, fractional solutions may still appear in the continuous relaxation. From that reformulation, we identify that the interaction between the leader variables and the follower dual variables, which we capture through a leader–potential set, is the key structure to be convexified to guarantee that a continuous relaxation recovers the optimal value of the original problem, closing the objective gap.
